title: Introduction to RPA and Microsoft Power Automate
summary: RPA (Robotic Process Automation) is a major branch of the automation world that you must understand, because many enterprises rely on it and it is a common job requirement. RPA tools - the big names are UiPath, Automation Anywhere, and Microsoft Powe
content:
# Introduction to RPA and Microsoft Power Automate ##### The bank that automated a mainframe from 1987 A large Indian private bank had a reconciliation process running on a terminal application older than most of its employees. Every night, an operator logged into a green-screen interface, typed account numbers, read balances, and re-keyed them into a modern reporting system. No API. No database access — the vendor contract forbade it. No possibility of replacement inside three years. They deployed an RPA bot. It logs in, types, reads the screen, and writes to the new system — exactly as the human did, at 4 a.m., without errors. The bank did not modernize anything. They automated the *interface*. That is **RPA (Robotic Process Automation)** in one story, and it explains why a technology that sounds primitive is a multi-billion-dollar industry: enterprises are full of systems that cannot be changed but must be integrated. Academic surveys of the field (Syed et al., 2020) describe RPA precisely this way — as a pragmatic layer over the "last mile" of legacy integration. ##### What RPA actually is RPA software mimics human interaction with a computer's user interface. A bot clicks buttons, types into fields, reads text from the screen, navigates menus, copies between applications, and handles files — driving the same GUI a person would. The three names you must know: **UiPath** — the market leader, headquartered in New York with major engineering in Bengaluru and Romania. Studio (the visual designer), Orchestrator (the management and scheduling server), and a large ecosystem. Dominant in banking, insurance and BPO. A free Community Edition exists for learning. **Automation Anywhere** — the other enterprise heavyweight, cloud-native architecture, strong in finance and healthcare. **Microsoft Power Automate** — the accessible one, and where you should start. It comes in two distinct products under one name: **cloud flows** (an iPaaS, direct competitor to Zapier) and **Power Automate Desktop** (true RPA that drives Windows applications). Desktop is included free with Windows 10 and 11, which makes it the easiest RPA on earth to try. **How RPA differs from what you have learned.** iPaaS tools talk to the *data layer* through APIs — structured, documented, fast. RPA talks to the *presentation layer* — the pixels and controls a human sees. That is both its unique power and its permanent weakness. ##### Attended versus unattended automation This distinction appears in every RPA job description, and it is what today's assignment asks you to explain. **Attended automation** runs on a person's machine, alongside them, usually started by them. Think of it as a power tool: the human is present, triggers the bot, and handles anything it cannot. - Triggered by a button, hotkey or the human opening a case. - Runs in the foreground on the user's desktop — they can watch it. - Can pause and ask a human for input or a decision. - Typical use: a call-centre agent presses a key and the bot pulls up the customer's records from four systems in three seconds instead of ninety. **Unattended automation** runs on a dedicated machine or virtual desktop with no human present, on a schedule or a queue. - Triggered by a timer, a file arriving, or an orchestrator dispatching work. - Runs headless overnight, at scale, across many virtual machines. - Must handle every exception itself — nobody is there to click "OK." - Typical use: the bank's 4 a.m. reconciliation; processing 12,000 invoices over a weekend. The engineering implications differ sharply. Unattended bots need robust error handling, credential vaults, logging, and orchestration infrastructure. Attended bots need good UX and graceful hand-back to the human. Most real deployments use both: attended bots assist staff during the day, unattended bots grind through volume at night. ##### Power Automate cloud flows Cloud flows will feel immediately familiar — they are Zapier with a Microsoft accent. Trigger, actions, connectors, expressions. The three flow types: - **Automated** — an event triggers it (new email, new SharePoint item, new Forms response). - **Instant** — a human triggers it (a button in Teams or the mobile app). - **Scheduled** — cron-like recurrence. Where Power Automate genuinely wins is **depth inside Microsoft 365**. If a business runs on Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Excel Online and Dataverse, the integration is tighter and cheaper than anything Zapier offers — and it is often already included in the licence they pay for. A flow is defined underneath as JSON. Here is the shape of today's practical task — email with attachment arrives, save to OneDrive, notify Teams: ```json { "definition": { "triggers": { "When_a_new_email_arrives_V3": { "type": "OpenApiConnection", "inputs": { "parameters": { "includeAttachments": true, "onlyWithAttachment": true, "folderPath": "Inbox" } } } }, "actions": { "Apply_to_each_attachment": { "type": "Foreach", "foreach": "@triggerOutputs()?['body/attachments']", "actions": { "Create_file": { "type": "OpenApiConnection", "inputs": { "parameters": { "folderPath": "/Invoices/@{formatDateTime(utcNow(),'yyyy/MM')}", "name": "@{items('Apply_to_each_attachment')?['name']}", "body": "@items('Apply_to_each_attachment')?['contentBytes']" } } } } }, "Post_message_in_Teams": { "type": "OpenApiConnection", "runAfter": { "Apply_to_each_attachment": ["Succeeded"] }, "inputs": { "parameters": { "messageBody": "Saved @{length(triggerOutputs()?['body/attachments'])} attachment(s) from @{triggerOutputs()?['body/from']}" } } } } } } ``` You will build this in the visual designer, not by hand — but reading the JSON shows you the structure: triggers, actions, a `Foreach` loop over attachments, `runAfter` dependencies, and expressions like `formatDateTime(utcNow(),'yyyy/MM')` for the dated folder. Two Power Automate concepts worth knowing early: **`runAfter`** lets an action run only when a previous one *failed* — that is how you build error branches. And the **Apply to each** loop appears automatically the moment you reference an array field, which surprises people the first time. ##### Desktop automation and UI interaction Power Automate Desktop is where it becomes real RPA. You record or build a sequence of desktop actions: ```text Launch Excel → Read from Excel worksheet → For each row → Launch legacy app → Populate text field "Account No" with %CurrentItem['account']% → Press button "Search" → Wait for window "Results" to appear → Extract data from window → %Balance% → Write to Excel cell (row, column D) = %Balance% → Close legacy app ``` The technique that determines whether this works reliably is **element selection**. Desktop RPA identifies controls in one of three ways, in descending order of robustness: 1. **UI element selectors** — the tool reads the application's accessibility tree and identifies a control by its automation ID, class and hierarchy. Robust; survives the window being moved or resized. Always prefer this. 2. **OCR / image matching** — the bot looks for a picture of a button on screen. Works when the accessibility tree is unavailable (Citrix sessions, remote desktops, Java applets, screenshots-as-UI). Fragile: breaks with resolution changes, theme changes, or a scrollbar appearing. 3. **Coordinate clicking** — "click at x=430, y=278." Almost always wrong. One resolution change and your bot clicks Delete instead of Save. The same waiting discipline from browser automation applies, only more so: **wait for a window or control to exist**, never a fixed sleep, and never assume an application opens instantly. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Business process to automate] --> B{Does the app have
an API or connector?} B -->|Yes| C[iPaaS / cloud flow
Zapier, Make, n8n, PA cloud] B -->|No| D{Is it a web app?} D -->|Yes| E[Browser automation
Playwright / Selenium] D -->|No, desktop or terminal| F{Human present
during the run?} F -->|Yes| G[Attended RPA
on the user's machine] F -->|No| H[Unattended RPA
scheduled VM + orchestrator] ``` ##### When RPA beats API-based automation Be honest about this: **API-first, always** — unless one of these applies. **1. No API exists and never will.** Legacy desktop software, mainframe green screens, vendor applications with locked-down contracts. This is RPA's core territory. **2. The API exists but is prohibitively restricted.** Some enterprise vendors charge enormous fees for API access, or the integration requires a procurement cycle measured in quarters. A bot on an existing licensed seat can be cheaper and faster to deploy. **3. The process spans many disconnected applications** in a way no single integration covers — copy from a PDF, paste into a desktop ERP, screenshot into an email. **4. Time-to-value matters more than elegance.** Replacing a legacy system takes eighteen months; an RPA bot takes two weeks. RPA is explicitly a bridge technology — Syed et al. call it a tactical rather than strategic solution — and that is a legitimate engineering choice when the strategic fix is years away. **5. Compliance requires the system of record be touched exactly as a human would**, with the same audit trail. The counter-argument you must also hold: RPA bots are **expensive to maintain**. Every UI change breaks them. Industry experience consistently shows maintenance consuming a large fraction of RPA programme budgets. A bot is a liability you are choosing to accept because the alternative is worse. ##### Common pitfalls - **Automating a broken process.** RPA amplifies whatever it copies. Fix and simplify the process first — this is the single most cited cause of failed RPA programmes. - **Coordinate-based clicking** instead of proper selectors. - **No exception handling in unattended bots** — a single unexpected dialog box halts an overnight run and nobody knows until morning. - **Hard-coded credentials** — use Power Automate's connection references or an enterprise credential vault, never plain text in a variable. - **Ignoring licensing.** Power Automate premium connectors, per-user vs per-flow plans, and unattended bot licences all cost real money. Check before you design. - **Screen resolution and DPI drift** on the bot VM breaking image-based steps. - **Choosing RPA when an API existed** because nobody checked. - **No monitoring** — bots must report success and failure like any other production system. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: create a free Microsoft account and build a **Power Automate cloud flow** — when an email with an attachment arrives, save it to OneDrive and post a Teams message — then run and test it. Notice how similar the mental model is to Zapier, and notice the differences: the automatic *Apply to each* loop over attachments, the expression language, the `runAfter` settings hidden under each action's menu. The mini project pushes into real RPA territory: combine a cloud flow with a **desktop flow** if you can. A good scoped version is a scheduled flow that reads rows from an Excel file, processes them, and writes results back — or, if you have a Windows machine, a desktop flow that drives a UI-only application (even Notepad or Calculator is a legitimate first target for learning selectors and waits). For the assignment, explain **attended versus unattended RPA** — trigger, location, human presence, exception handling, typical use case — and write a **decision note on when RPA beats an API-based tool**, with two concrete examples. The legacy-mainframe case and the multi-application copy-paste case are strong choices. Make the note honest: include the maintenance cost, because a recommendation that acknowledges its own downside is far more credible. ##### Key takeaways - RPA automates the user interface rather than the data layer, which is why it can integrate systems that have no API at all. - UiPath and Automation Anywhere lead the enterprise market; Power Automate is the accessible entry point, with cloud flows (iPaaS) and Desktop (true RPA) under one name. - Attended bots assist a present human on their machine; unattended bots run scheduled and headless, and must handle every exception themselves. - Element selection determines reliability: prefer accessibility-tree selectors, use OCR/image matching only when forced, and never click by coordinates. - Choose API-based automation first; use RPA deliberately as a bridge for legacy and multi-application processes, and budget for its ongoing maintenance.
